title: wiretap: Do not silently limit capture length
description:
Libpcap assumes that packet length is greater or equal to captured data
length. However, due to a bug in libpcap, it is possible for libpcap to
generate isochronous URB packets (WTAP_ENCAP_USB_LINUX_MMAPPED) with
captured data length greater than packet length. The discrepancy comes
from slightly different semantics in Linux kernel.

Linux kernel usbmon packet documentation mentions:
    unsigned int length;  /* 32: Length of data (submitted or actual) */
    unsigned int len_cap; /* 36: Delivered length */

Wireshark shows usbmon packet length as URB length (usb.urb_len) and
len_cap as Data length (usb.data_len). For usbmon isochronous IN packets
containing data (URB complete), usbmon length is "actual". Actual length
is the sum of payload packets length received from device. Delivered
length refers to the amount of data associated with usbmon packet, that
is the isochronous descriptors and actual isochronous data. There can be
multiple isochronous descriptors in single URB and the actual payload in
special cases can be noncontiguous (there can be gaps).

Libpcap when reading usbmon capture calculates packet length based on
usbmon packet structure size (64), "actual length" and number of
isochronous descriptors. This gives expected packet length as long as
there are no gaps between isochronous data. If there are gaps, the
calculated packet length will be smaller than delivered length.

Wireshark should show the frame length and captured length as provided
by the capture engine, even if the capture length is greater than frame
length. Silently limiting captured length essentially hides the issue
from the user and allows misbehaving capture engine to go unnoticed.

Passing unmodified Frame Length and Capture Length to dissectors (and
thus complete tvb) allows USB dissector to show all ISO Data fields
captured on Linux usbmon interface using bugged libpcap.

Fixes #18021

notes.body: requested review from @guyharris
assigned to @desowin
mentioned in issue #18021

> Length refers to the payload length transmitted on the bus,

Not if the packet data doesn't exactly match what's transmitted on the bus, with the possible addition of a metadata header.

And if there *is* a metadata header - or any additional data - added over and above what's on the bus, its length should be included in the captured length *AND* the actual length.

> The len_cap includes ISO descriptors and potential padding (and length does not as it only refers to the actual payload).

It *shouldn't* refer to the actual payload.  If a payload length is important, and can't just be calculated by subtracting the amount of "extra" stuff from the length, it should be provided in a metadata header, so that a packet analyzer can display it.

> > Length refers to the payload length transmitted on the bus,
> 
> Not if the packet data doesn't exactly match what's transmitted on the bus, with the possible addition of a metadata header.

I should somehow reword it to make it clear that the "Length" in that sentence (and len_cap) refers to struct usbmon_packet:

```
	unsigned int length;	/* 32: Length of data (submitted or actual) */
	unsigned int len_cap;	/* 36: Delivered length */
```

> And if there *is* a metadata header - or any additional data - added over and above what's on the bus, its length should be included in the captured length *AND* the actual length.

This refers to how pcap format works and it is libpcap here that does not respect that with regard to isochronous URBs retrieved on usbmon interface.
There is a semantic clash between usbmon and libpcap. The end result is that the libpcap writes pcap packets with incorrectly set length (based on perfectly fine data from usbmon interface).

> This refers to how pcap format works and it is libpcap here that does not respect that with regard to isochronous URBs retrieved on usbmon interface.

Then it needs to be fixed to do so.

The length value for a packet in a pcap or pcapng file should reflect how many bytes of packet data would've been in that record if no snapshot length or buffer size limitation in the capture mechanism had caused any data to be discarded

> The length value for a packet in a pcap or pcapng file should reflect how many bytes of packet data would've been in that record if no snapshot length or buffer size limitation in the capture mechanism had caused any data to be discarded

Yes, that is perfectly understandable and clear.

Now we have situation where libpcap has been producing isochronous URB packets with incorrect packet length for years. It should be somehow handled in Wireshark. Silently limiting capture length to packet length is not proper solution as it *hides* the problem instead of fixing it.

As far the actual code change goes, I believe this Merge Request is correct. It lets meticulous user notice that something fishy is going on, while at the same time allowing the USB dissector get all data present in the capture file.

The commit message is not so good, but that in general reflects my limited English skills (or more of a clear communication, as I would have difficulty describing it clearly also in my native language).
I have updated the commit message in a way that is hopefully clearer.

> Now we have situation where libpcap has been producing isochronous URB packets with incorrect packet length for years. It should be somehow handled in Wireshark.

...and libpcap, for programs *other* than Wireshark.

If the correct length value can be computed from values in the metadata header, then both libpcap's and libwiretap's pcap-common.c code should, for `LINKTYPE_USB_LINUX` and `LINKTYPE_USB_LINUX_MMAPPED` files, check whether caplen > len and, if so, recalculate the len and provide that to the caller.  (There's already link-type-specific code to deal with metadata headers in host byte order, so this would be done at the same time.)

If by "metadata header" you mean the 64 bytes usbmon packet header, then correct length value cannot be computed from values in the metadata header. To compute the value the ISO descriptors have to be processed, but depending on snaplen, these might be unavailable. Note that usbmon `cap_len` can already be limited, and the only way to know the "total sum of gaps" is to infer it from ISO descriptors.

It also depends what "handling" means. In case of Wireshark, I believe "handling" is more of "show the truth" than "sweep it under the carpet". In this particular case, showing the truth is what this Merge Request does, i.e. "Frame Length" and "Capture Length" are equal to the values stored in capture file.

If for whatever reason the incorrect value hinders further dissection and Wireshark has to use some other value instead, such action should be accompanied with expert info.

> "show the truth"

What does "truth" mean in this context?

pcap format was originally designed for network captures, such as Ethernet captures, in which 1) there are no metadata headers and 2) the payload is a link-layer packet.  pcapng was designed after some pcap link-layer header types didn't follow those principles, but still has the same model.  

In that model, the notion is that:

- a capture may include "slicing", in which data at the end of the packet may be "sliced off" and discarded, so that it's no passed to the capturing program (and maybe not to userland at all);
- the "length" is the number of octets in the link-layer packet before any slicing occurred;
- the "captured length" is the number of octets in the link-layer packet after slicing occurred.

In that case, the "captured length" is always <= the "length".

That property can be used by packet analyzers, when they detect that they can't dissect any further because they've run out of data to dissect, to determine whether the problem is "the snapshot length specified for the capture was too small to capture all the data in the packet you're looking at", which is *not* an indication of a malformed packet, or "the packet isn't as large as it should be in this particular case", which *is* an indication of a malformed packet.

tcpdump doesn't *currently* make that distinction, but - especially now that it uses the same setjmp/longjmp-based bounds checking and error reporting that Wireshark does - it could conceivably do that in the future.  The biggest issue I see with that is to distinguish between the two without overly surprising people who have learned what "[!{protocol name}]" means in tcpdump output.

Wireshark *does* make that distinction.  (It also has other mechanisms, using information above the capture-file layer, to distinguish between "that's the first fragment of an unreassembled higher-level PDU, and we ran off the end of that fragment", which *also* isn't an indication of a malformed packet *and* isn't an indication that the specified snapshot length for the capture was too small.)

Some link-layer types that don't match that Ethernet-ish model are:

ATM - if a "packet" is, for example, an AAL5 PDU, the packet payload is the result of reassembly, not a collection of raw cells on the network.

802.11 - various forms of radio metadata are present, and there's also the A-MPDU stuff.

Bluetooth HCI - those are "what you send to and receive from the host controller", not "what gets sent over the air".

and, of course...

USB - many of the link-layer types for USB are like Bluetooth HCI, in that they correspond to transfers between the host and the USB adapter, rather than transfers over USB.

In those cases, the length isn't just "length on the medium", as the packet in the capture file may have gone over the medium in multiple link-layer packets, or may have additional metadata preceding the "raw" packet data.

So how to generalize "captured length" and "length"?

"Captured length" is, given the way the file formats are defined, the number of octets of "packet data", including metadata headers, and not reflecting any division of the packet into link-layer packets on the medium.

The simplest generalization of "length" would be "how big that would be if no slicing had been done", i.e. if the snapshot length had been 2^32-1 (as the length fields are 32-bit unsigned quantities - if we need to deal with packets bigger than that, we're going to need a ~~bigger boat~~ new capture file format).

Linux usbmon adds another complication, as it has *another* truncation mechanism separate from a user-specified snapshot length.  `mon_bin_event()` in drivers/usb/mon/mon_bin.c does:

```
	/* not an issue unless there's a subtle bug in a HCD somewhere */
	if (length >= urb->transfer_buffer_length)
		length = urb->transfer_buffer_length;

	if (length >= rp->b_size/5)
		length = rp->b_size/5;
```

which limits the amount of data it copies to the buffer (other than the fixed-length metadata header) to `rp->b_size/5`.  `b_size` is the size of the ring buffer; it defaults to `CHUNK_ALIGN(300*1024)` and cannot be set larger than `CHUNK_ALIGN(1200*1024)`  (`CHUNK_ALIGN()` rounds up to a page size.)

So, ideally, if "how big a packet you would have gotten had I not done

```
	if (length >= rp->b_size/5)
		length = rp->b_size/5;
```

before copying" can be determined, the value of "length" could be calculated.

If not, then at least "set length to captured length if captured length > length" would preserve the "captured length" <= "length" property.  (It still raises the question of whether the way the Linux USB libpcap code calculates "length" is bogus.)

As for reading pcap and pcapng files, "set length to captured length if captured length > length" would fix that problem.

So does "truth" mean:

- "the captured length was greater than the length in the capture file", which is technically true, but I'm unconvinced it's of any interest once we've fixed the problem - it's interesting only in that it points out that we're miscalculating length;
- "here's the length value calculated by the Linux code for usbmon";
- something else?

> > > "show the truth"
> 
> What does "truth" mean in this context?

The truth refers to what the capture file contains or what Wireshark was provided with by the capture engine.

> USB - many of the link-layer types for USB are like Bluetooth HCI, in that they correspond to transfers between the host and the USB adapter, rather than transfers over USB.

Yes. Most of the "USB" types are really URB (USB Request Block) that are OS specific. The URB is essentially an order for USB host controller to either deliver or pick up data from the device on terms described by USB specification. But each "URB company" (Linux usbmon, Windows USBPcap, Darwin) has has its own order forms (URB structures).

The LINKTYPE_USB_2_0 (and the [speed specific linktypes that I propose](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/libpcap/pull/1109) to deal with inherent USB layering violations) is the only USB link type that really contains the USB packets.

> In those cases, the length isn't just "length on the medium", as the packet in the capture file may have gone over the medium in multiple link-layer packets, or may have additional metadata preceding the "raw" packet data.

The length is hardly comparable :-) The URB structure is really arbitrary and never makes it on the medium.  There's a lot of NAKs involved on the medium. Excluding the NAKed transactions, the overhead on medium is generally much less than the URB structure unless the buffer associated with URB is large.

> So how to generalize "captured length" and "length"?
> 
> "Captured length" is, given the way the file formats are defined, the number of octets of "packet data", including metadata headers, and not reflecting any division of the packet into link-layer packets on the medium.

Yes.

> The simplest generalization of "length" would be "how big that would be if no slicing had been done", i.e. if the snapshot length had been 2^32-1 (as the length fields are 32-bit unsigned quantities - if we need to deal with packets bigger than that, we're going to need a ~~bigger boat~~ new capture file format).

Yes.

> Linux usbmon adds another complication [...]

Yes, that greatly complicates the way to achieve pcap format "length" and "captured length".

> If not, then at least "set length to captured length if captured length > length" would preserve the "captured length" <= "length" property. (It still raises the question of whether the way the Linux USB libpcap code calculates "length" is bogus.)

Pretty much the only way to allow Linux USB libpcap code to come up with "length" and "captured length" (that adheres to pcap format specification) is to compact the buffer to remove gaps. If libpcap was compacting it would always know how much data it would have written even if the isochronous descriptors themselves were capture limited by usbmon.

> As for reading pcap and pcapng files, "set length to captured length if captured length > length" would fix that problem.

It would hide the problem, making it harder for users to notice there is something wrong with their capture engine.

> So does "truth" mean:
> 
> * "the captured length was greater than the length in the capture file", which is technically true, but I'm unconvinced it's of any interest once we've fixed the problem - it's interesting only in that it points out that we're miscalculating length;

This is crucial in my opinion. Otherwise the user gets false impression that everything is fine, while in reality there is a systematic problem in the capture engine.

I was fooled by Wireshark to believe the capture file #18021 was simply snaplen limited, while in reality it was libpcap that wrongly set the length.

The problem can be fixed in libpcap, sure. But fixing the now known bug in libpcap is completely separate to *identifying* that other capture engines can misbehave in the same way as libpcap did.

> The length is hardly comparable :-) The URB structure is really arbitrary and never makes it on the medium. There's a lot of NAKs involved on the medium. Excluding the NAKed transactions, the overhead on medium is generally much less than the URB structure unless the buffer associated with URB is large.

In other words, the length isn't "length on the medium", exactly as I said.

> Pretty much the only way to allow Linux USB libpcap code to come up with "length" and "captured length" (that adheres to pcap format specification) is to compact the buffer to remove gaps.

If that's the case - i.e., if "captured length" currently doesn't correspond to the number of payload bytes, as is required in order to be able to read a pcap file past the first packet - we have a *real* problem.

If "compact the buffer to remove gaps" alludes to the comment before `mon_bin_collate_isodesc()` in mon_bin.c:

```
/*
 * This is the look-ahead pass in case of 'C Zi', when actual_length cannot
 * be used to determine the length of the whole contiguous buffer.
 */
```

then `ep->len_cap` is set to `length + lendesc` after `length` has been initially calculated.  `lenses` is `ndesc*sizeof(struct mon_bin_isodesc)`, i.e. the total length of the isochronous descriptors, so we can calculate the value of `length` from the `len_cap` field.  That's the `data_len` field in the libpcap code's version of the header; caplen is computed from that:

- first, `clen` is set to `max_clen`, which is set to `handle->snapshot - sizeof(pcap_usb_header_mmapped)`, i.e. the maximum amount of data *following* the metadata header that we should claim is available to libpcap's caller in order to implement the snapshot length;
- then, if `data_len` is < `clen`, `clen` is set to `data_len`, i.e. `min(data_len, max_clen)`.

So, if `length` is the amount of data copied into the memory-mapped buffer after the metadata header and isochronous descriptors, then `clen` is set to what the captured length should be.

So, for the length, we want to do the same calculation, except with whatever value `length` had *before* it was clamped inside the usbmon kernel code.

In `mon_bin_event()`, `length` is initially set to `usb_len`, which, in the version of the metadata header in libpcap, is the `urb_len` field.

Then, it gets adjusted for isochronous transfers.  If the endpoint is isochronous, the event type is `'C'` (that's the `event_type` field in the libpcap version of the metadata header), and the direction is "incoming" (indicated by the uppermost bit being set in the `endpoint_number` field of the libpcap version of the metadata header), then `length` is set to the result of `mon_bin_collate_isodesc()`, which we can duplicate by scanning the isochronous descriptors to find the largest value for the sum of the `offset` and `len` fields (if there are no descriptors, the length is 0).  After that, it's reduced for truncation purposes, which we don't want to do when we calculate `length`.

We can also do that when reading a Linux USB packet, to fix up the damage from libpcap doing it incorrectly. Doing that does *not* hide a problem, it *fixes* a problem.

> But fixing the now known bug in libpcap is completely separate to *identifying* that other capture engines can misbehave in the same way as libpcap did.

Then we should *identify* it in Wireshark by having libwiretap either 1) return an error if caplen > len, *explicitly indicating to the user what the problem is*, or adding the ability to return a warning indication, again explicitly indicating to the user what the problem is, and then setting len to caplen so that the dissection can at least proceed semi-sanely.

> If that's the case - i.e., if "captured length" currently doesn't correspond to the number of payload bytes, as is required in order to be able to read a pcap file past the first packet - we have a *real* problem.

I don't know what would happen if the capture was directly saved to pcap format instead of pcapng. Here however, regardless of the format, the Captured Length is correct, only the Packet Length is wrong.

Currently if you open capture file from #18021 in Wireshark and save it to pcap format, Wireshark will silently truncate captured data, meaning the ISO Data for USB isodesc 6 and 7 in Packet 33 won't be there at all in the new file, and USB isodesc 5 data will only partially be there.

> So, for the length, we want to do the same calculation, except with whatever value `length` had *before* it was clamped inside the usbmon kernel code.
> 
> In `mon_bin_event()`, `length` is initially set to `usb_len`, which, in the version of the metadata header in libpcap, is the `urb_len` field.
> 
> Then, it gets adjusted for isochronous transfers. If the endpoint is isochronous, the event type is `'C'` (that's the `event_type` field in the libpcap version of the metadata header), and the direction is "incoming" (indicated by the uppermost bit being set in the `endpoint_number` field of the libpcap version of the metadata header), then `length` is set to the result of `mon_bin_collate_isodesc()`, which we can duplicate by scanning the isochronous descriptors to find the largest value for the sum of the `offset` and `len` fields (if there are no descriptors, the length is 0). After that, it's reduced for truncation purposes, which we don't want to do when we calculate `length`.

This can be only done if the isochronous descriptors were not capture limited.

> We can also do that when reading a Linux USB packet, to fix up the damage from libpcap doing it incorrectly. Doing that does *not* hide a problem, it *fixes* a problem.

Applying such fixup, atleast in Wireshark, should be accompanied with expert info. User should have easy method to get information about such fixups happening under the hood.

> > But fixing the now known bug in libpcap is completely separate to *identifying* that other capture engines can misbehave in the same way as libpcap did.
> 
> Then we should *identify* it in Wireshark by having libwiretap either 1) return an error if caplen > len, *explicitly indicating to the user what the problem is*, or adding the ability to return a warning indication, again explicitly indicating to the user what the problem is, and then setting len to caplen so that the dissection can at least proceed semi-sanely.

If you compile Wireshark with this Merge Request, open capture file from #18021 and navigate to Frame 33 you will see Frame Length and Capture Length equal to the values present in pcap file (576 for Frame Length and 744 for Capture Length). The USB dissector will get 744 bytes of data, meaning all data present in capture is shown.

Without this Merge Request, Wireshark just shows Frame Length and Capture Length equal to 576 bytes. The USB dissector gets 576 bytes of data, meaning that Frame 33 ISO desc 5, 6 and 7 do not have the ISO Data shown even though it is present in the capture file.

My goal is to have Frame Length and Capture Length shown by Wireshark Frame dissector is equal to the values present in pcap file *and* USB dissector getting all data available. This Merge Request achieves the goal. I don't quite know how to achieve the goal without removing the clamping in wiretap code (clamping it the other direction, i.e. set Packet Length to Capture Length, would only partially achieve the goal).

> I don't know what would happen if the capture was directly saved to pcap format instead of pcapng.

There is precisely zero difference between the way this works with pcap and the way this works with pcapng.  The captured length and length mean exactly the same thing.

> Currently if you open capture file from #18021 in Wireshark ... Packet 33

In the raw pcapng capture file, the captured length of packet 33 is 744 and the purported actual length is 576, which is utterly and totally bogus, and does not reflect any "truth" other than "it is a true statement that this packet, in this file, has a miscalculated, and non-useful and misleading, length".

*That* truth should be reported directly to the user in a fashion that clearly indicates that they are the victim in a bug in whatever code wrote that file, rather than requiring them to deduce that by seeing length < captured length.

If any dissection of that packet is done by Wireshark, the initial rebuff for the packet data should ***NOT*** have a captured length of 744 and a length of 576, as that makes it impossible for the packet to be correctly dissected with appropriate error reporting.

The way that the captured length was computed in libpcap is that, in `usb_read_linux_mmap()` in pcap-usb-linux.c:

1. `max_clen` is set to `handle->snapshot - sizeof(pcap_usb_header_mmapped)` - from the Capture Summary, `handle->snapshot` was 245824, and `sizeof(pcap_usb_header_mmapped)` is 64, so that's 245760.
2. `clen` is set to `max_clen`, hence 245760.
3. If `hdr->data_len` is < `clen`, `clen` is set to `hdr->data_len`.  `hdr->data_len` is the "Data length [bytes]" field in the metadata, which is 680 in packet 33, so `clen` is now set to 680.
4. The captured length is set to `sizeof(pcap_usb_header_mmapped) + clen`, which is 680+64, or 744.

The way that the length was computed in libpcap is that, in `usb_read_linux_mmap()` in pcap-usb-linux.c:

1. The "Data" flag in the metadata is checked; it's 0 in that packet, meaning - confusingly - that data is present.
2. Given that, the length is calculated as `sizeof(pcap_usb_header_mmapped) + (hdr->ndesc * sizeof (usb_isodesc)) + hdr->urb_len`.  `hdr->ndesc` is the `Number of ISO descriptors` field, hence 8, and `sizeof (usb_isodesc)` is 16, so the product is 128.  `hdr->usb_len` is the "URB length [bytes]" field, hence 384.  Thus, the length is 64 + 128 + 384, or 576.

This is clearly wrong, as it's literally impossible for there to be more captured data than total data - you can't fill a 744-litre barrel with the fluid from a 576-litre barrel.

If we look at how the actual length of data to copy is calculated in the usbmon driver, we see, in `mon_bin_event()` in mon_bin.c:

1. `length` is set to `urb_length`, which is also the value put into the the "URB length [bytes]" field in the metadata header, hence 384.
2. If the endpoint is isochronous, which it is, the event type is `'C'`, which it is (the "URB type" field in the metadata header is set to the event type, and it's `'C'`), and if the direction is "in", which it is (the direction is the 0x80 bit of the endpoint/direction field in the metadata header), then `length` is set to the result of `mon_bin_collate_isodesc()`, which is the largest sum of offset and length in all the isochronous descriptors.  The largest value is in the last descriptor, which is the offset ("Offset [bytes]" field), or 504, plus the length ("Length [bytes]"), or 48, hence 552.
3. `length` is then, possibly, truncated.

The "Data length [bytes]" field is set to `length` plus `lendesc`; `lendesc` is the total number of bytes of descriptors, hence 128.  The "Data length [bytes]" field is 680, so `length` was calculated as 552, meaning no truncation was done.

"No truncation was done" means "the captured length and the length should be the same, and both should be the amount of data provided."  I.e., they both *should* have been 744.

The fact that they *weren't* both 744 is a libpcap bug; the bug is in the way it calculates the length.

If libpcap were to reproduce the way `length` is calculated, *before* it gets trimmed, it would:

1. Start out by setting it to the value of the "URB length [bytes]" field in the metadata header, hence 384.
2. If the endpoint is isochronous, the event type ("URB type" field in the metadata header) is `'C'`, and if the direction (the direction is the 0x80 bit of the endpoint/direction field in the metadata header) is "in", calculate the largest offset+length value in the isochronous descriptors, and see the length to that.

Then, it would add to that the total length of the isochronous descriptors ("Number of ISO descriptors" times the 16-byte size of a descriptor) and the length of the metadata header, and use *that* as the length.

I've tested a version of libpcap that does that; I didn't have any isochronous transfers for which to test the capture fixes, but it does correctly set the length for other transfers.

That version also fixes up the length field when reading pcap or pcapng files; running tcpdump, linked with that version, to read the pcapng file with the incorrect lengths and write to a pcap file produces a pcap file with the right lengths.  That file reads and dissects correctly in Wireshark.

> This can be only done if the isochronous descriptors were not capture limited.

If by "capture limited" you mean that there are so many of the 16-byte descriptors between the metadata header and the raw data that they don't fit within the limit imposed by the capture mechanism, then the maximum size can be calculated from the available descriptors and, if that's greater than the value of `usb_len`, we use it to calculate the length.

If, however, you're referring to the data to which the descriptors refer, and all the descriptors *do* fit in the captured data, then we can calculate the length from the descriptors - that's what libpcap now does.

> > This can be only done if the isochronous descriptors were not capture limited.
> 
> If by "capture limited" you mean that there are so many of the 16-byte descriptors between the metadata header and the raw data that they don't fit within the limit imposed by the capture mechanism, then the maximum size can be calculated from the available descriptors and, if that's greater than the value of `usb_len`, we use it to calculate the length.

Calculating Packet Length using the last available descriptor gives Packet Length that is always greater than Captured Length (so the bug where Captured Length > Packet Length is generated by libpcap is fixed). However, when not all descriptors were available to libpcap (but the descriptors definitely were available to usbmon), then the calculated Packet Length will be shorter than what it would have been if usbmon did not truncate the buffer.

> However, when not all descriptors were available to libpcap (but the descriptors definitely were available to usbmon),

There are two cases where this would be the case:

1. this is a live capture, and there are *so* many descriptors that usbmon discards them;
2. this is reading a capture file for a capture for which the specified snaplen is so short that, even though all the descriptors were made available to libpcap, the snaplen wass small enough that the captured length provided to the caller was such that it didn't include all the descriptors, so they weren't written to the file.

The first requires a very large number of descriptors; the latter requires either a very large number of descriptors or a very small snapshot length.  Neither are, I suspect, very likely.

> then the calculated Packet Length will be shorter than what it would have been if usbmon did not truncate the buffer.

In either of the two cases listed above, it is, sadly, literally impossible to calculate the correct length, as the capture mechanism doesn't provide the pre-truncation value of `length` in the metadata header.

However, the largest of:

- the existing value;
- the "captured length" (which is calculated from `data_len`, which is, in turn, based on all of the descriptors made available to usbmon, but is reduced as a result of the limit usbmon imposes on the amount of data it supplies to userland)
- the "length calculated from the descriptors we have" (which is based on a subset of the descriptors, but isn't reduced as a result of the limit usbmon imposes);

would be the closest value to the length that we can get, is guaranteed to be >= the captured length, and, as such, is an improvement over either of the other values.

> In either of the two cases listed above, it is, sadly, literally impossible to calculate the correct length, as the capture mechanism doesn't provide the pre-truncation value of `length` in the metadata header.

This is exactly the reason why I wrote "Pretty much the only way to allow Linux USB libpcap code to come up with "length" and "captured length" (that adheres to pcap format specification) is to compact the buffer to remove gaps. If libpcap was compacting it would always know how much data it would have written even if the isochronous descriptors themselves were capture limited by usbmon." in [comment above](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7057#note_970375455).

Such thing however cannot be applied retroactively to existing captures and could only be done to newly written captures. Not sure if it would be appropriate to perform such action under the existing linktype or if it would require new linktype.

> If libpcap was compacting it would always know how much data it would have written

Presumably meaning that, if the buffer is compacted - so that for all the descriptors, the offset of descriptor 0 is equal to 0, and the offset+len of descriptor N is equal to the offset of descriptor N+1 - the urb_len value would indicate how much data would have been written, as there would have been no padding between chunks of isochronous data.

That would also mean that the descriptors could be written out as 4 bytes of status and 4 bytes of length, as the offsets can be calculated from the lengths, and the padding wouldn't be necessary to align the descriptors on 8-byte boundaries or whatever it's there for.

> Not sure if it would be appropriate to perform such action under the existing linktype or if it would require new linktype.

As long as we modify the offsets so that the offset of descriptor 0 is equal to 0, and the offset+len of descriptor N is equal to the offset of descriptor N+1, any existing code that makes no assumptions about how many extra bytes are between the chunks of data to which an isochronous descriptor refers - i.e., that always looks at the Nth descriptor's offset to determine where its data begins - should Just Work.

Doing that would, however, involve extra copying over and above what's currently performed.

The libpcap issue was fixed in: [08ab69f4fc5d432eb7de26ee8e33b40ea4b79744](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/libpcap/commit/08ab69f4fc5d432eb7de26ee8e33b40ea4b79744), [b4eeafb93955807464d8bb9327772fb217fcdd9a](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/libpcap/commit/b4eeafb93955807464d8bb9327772fb217fcdd9a) and [e2c0fd75e48a3cbf1bf48b8afe28fff50d8e0877](https://github.com/the-tcpdump-group/libpcap/commit/e2c0fd75e48a3cbf1bf48b8afe28fff50d8e0877)

commits_data.title: wiretap: Do not silently limit capture length
commits_data.message:
wiretap: Do not silently limit capture length

Libpcap assumes that packet length is greater or equal to captured data
length. However, due to a bug in libpcap, it was possible for libpcap to
generate isochronous URB packets (WTAP_ENCAP_USB_LINUX_MMAPPED) with
captured data length greater than packet length. The discrepancy comes
from slightly different semantics in Linux kernel.

Linux kernel usbmon packet documentation mentions:
    unsigned int length;  /* 32: Length of data (submitted or actual) */
    unsigned int len_cap; /* 36: Delivered length */

Wireshark shows usbmon packet length as URB length (usb.urb_len) and
len_cap as Data length (usb.data_len). For usbmon isochronous IN packets
containing data (URB complete), usbmon length is "actual". Actual length
is the sum of payload packets length received from device. Delivered
length refers to the amount of data associated with usbmon packet, that
is the isochronous descriptors and actual isochronous data. There can be
multiple isochronous descriptors in single URB and the actual payload in
special cases can be noncontiguous (there can be gaps).

Libpcap when reading usbmon capture calculates packet length based on
usbmon packet structure size (64), "actual length" and number of
isochronous descriptors. This gives expected packet length as long as
there are no gaps between isochronous data. If there are gaps, the
calculated packet length will be smaller than delivered length.

Wireshark should show the frame length and captured length as provided
by the capture engine, even if the capture length is greater than frame
length. Silently limiting captured length essentially hides the issue
from the user and allows misbehaving capture engine to go unnoticed.

Passing unmodified Frame Length and Capture Length to dissectors (and
thus complete tvb) allows USB dissector to show all ISO Data fields
captured on Linux usbmon interface using bugged libpcap.

Fixes #18021
